proof_derivations: exp(t)>0 gives denominator>0. Division cancellation gives p*(1+exp(t))=1 and p*exp(t)>0, hence 0<p<1.
(p-1/2)^2>=0 implies p-p^2<=1/4; nonnegative factors prove the lower coefficient bound.
Cauchy-Schwarz gives dot(v,d_i)^2<=sum(v_j^2)*sum(d_ij^2). Multiply by nonnegative c<=1/4, sum over i, and multiply by 1/n>0. Add mu*sum(v_j^2). No curvature bound or contraction is a premise.

For real scalar loss, differentiation of exp composed with negation and log gives -exp(-t)/(1+exp(-t)). Exp-neg and nonzero-denominator algebra identify this as -p(t); inverse differentiation gives p_prime=-c.

Differentiate finite coordinate polynomial squares and each finite loss summand along w+t*v. Then differentiate the explicit first derivative again. Finite sum rules and chain rules identify the exact second directional derivative with Q; Q bounds then apply to the actual stated real objective.

Interchange finite coordinate and pair sums to identify the explicit coordinate gradient with the first line derivative at zero. This is a derived identity for the real objective, not a premise about a native gradient.

For a scalar twice differentiable function with actual second derivative bounded by C, q(t)=C*t^2/2-f(t) has nonnegative second derivative. Mathlib scalar convexity gives q_prime(0)<=slope(q,0,1), which rearranges to f(1)<=f(0)+f_prime(0)+C/2. The objective theorem supplies C=L*||v||^2 from the previously established actual second derivative and Q bound.

Substitute v=-eta*g into the proved upper Taylor bound. Coordinate sum-of-squares scaling gives ||v||^2=eta^2*||g||^2 and dot(g,v)=-eta*||g||^2. For mu>0, mean L is positive; eta<=1/L and eta>=0 imply eta*(1-eta*L/2)>=eta/2. No desired descent or contraction inequality is assumed.

The original profile bridge proves finite Rat indexing/norm/mean equalities by closed kernel reduction, casts finite sums through additive homomorphism laws, and proves every Real coordinate norm and mean-L equality. Positivity and safe-step products transfer through the order embedding of rationals into reals. Thus original curvature/descent instantiation has no unproved coordinate-alignment premise.
